subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, while electrons orbit around it.

questions.q: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
questions.explain: A neutron is electrically neutral, so its relative charge is 0.

questions.q: An alpha particle is identical to which of the following?
questions.explain: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, made up of 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

questions.q: A beta particle is best described as...
options: a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
questions.explain: A beta-minus particle is a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron changes into a proton.

questions.q: Which type of nuclear radiation is stopped by a thin sheet of paper?
questions.explain: Alpha radiation is the least penetrating and is stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: Two isotopes of the same element always have...
options: the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
different numbers of protons and electrons
questions.explain: Isotopes have the same proton (atomic) number but different numbers of neutrons, giving different mass numbers.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, how do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number decreases by 4, atomic number decreases by 2
Mass number decreases by 2, atomic number decreases by 4
Mass number unchanged, atomic number increases by 1
Mass number decreases by 4, atomic number increases by 2
questions.explain: Losing an alpha particle (2 protons and 2 neutrons) reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits a beta-minus particle, what happens inside the nucleus?
options: A neutron changes into a proton
A proton changes into a neutron
Two protons and two neutrons are ejected
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron turns into a proton, emitting an electron (the beta particle).

questions.q: A nucleus of radium-226 (mass number 226, atomic number 88) decays by emitting an alpha particle. What are the mass number and atomic number of the nucleus produced?
questions.explain: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4 (226 to 222) and the atomic number by 2 (88 to 86).

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive source is measured in which unit?
questions.explain: Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq), where 1 Bq is one nuclear decay per second.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for...
options: half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay
all of the nuclei to decay
the mass of the sample to halve
the sample to become completely safe
questions.explain: Half-life is the average time for half of the remaining undecayed nuclei (or the activity) to halve.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as a random process because...
options: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or exactly when
every nucleus decays at a fixed regular time
decay only happens when the sample is heated
questions.explain: Decay is random: we cannot say which nucleus will decay or precisely when, only the probability over time.

questions.q: A radioactive source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. What is its activity after 6 hours?
questions.explain: 6 hours is 3 half-lives, so the activity halves three times: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 Bq.

questions.q: The count rate from a source falls from 240 counts/s to 30 counts/s in 9 hours. What is the half-life?
questions.explain: Going from 240 to 30 is a fall of three halvings (240 to 120 to 60 to 30), so 9 hours divided by 3 gives a half-life of 3 hours.

questions.q: A sample contains 1600 undecayed nuclei. After how many half-lives will only 200 undecayed nuclei remain?
questions.explain: 1600 halves to 800, then 400, then 200, which is three half-lives.

questions.q: Which of these is commonly used as a fuel in nuclear fission reactors?
questions.explain: Uranium-235 is a common fission fuel because its large nucleus can be split by absorbing a neutron.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion is the main process that releases energy in...
questions.explain: Fusion of light nuclei releases the energy that powers stars, including the Sun.

questions.q: Nuclear fission is best described as...
options: a large nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy
two small nuclei joining to form a larger nucleus
a nucleus emitting an alpha particle
an electron being absorbed by a nucleus
questions.explain: Fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.

questions.q: Nuclear fusion involves...
options: two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
a heavy nucleus splitting into two lighter nuclei
a nucleus emitting a beta particle
an atom losing an outer electron
questions.explain: Fusion joins light nuclei (such as hydrogen isotopes) into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy, and needs very high temperatures and pressures.

questions.q: In a nuclear fission chain reaction, the reaction is sustained because...
options: neutrons released by one fission go on to cause further fissions
electrons are released and absorbed by other nuclei
protons are ejected and split more nuclei
questions.explain: Each fission releases neutrons that can be absorbed by other nuclei, causing further fissions in a chain reaction.
